text: Privacy by Design flips the usual order: instead of building a system and then bolting privacy controls on afterward, you bake privacy into the architecture from the first design decision. This lesson covers all seven of its principles, and the exact way one became binding EU law.

Ann Cavoukian, Ontario's former Information and Privacy Commissioner, developed seven Foundational Principles. Proactive, not reactive, anticipate privacy problems before they happen. Privacy as the default setting, protection comes automatically, not buried in a settings menu. Privacy embedded into design, it's core architecture, not an add-on. Full functionality, positive-sum, not zero-sum, you shouldn't have to trade away features or security to get privacy.

The remaining three: end-to-end security, strong protection through the entire data lifecycle, from collection to secure destruction. Visibility and transparency, practices should be visible and verifiable to users, operators, and regulators, not hidden in fine print. And respect for user privacy, keeping the individual's interests at the center, with strong defaults and genuine user-friendliness.

GDPR Article 25 took this design philosophy and wrote it directly into binding law: data protection by design and by default. Organizations must build protection into their processing from the outset, and configure systems so that, by default, only the data necessary for a specific purpose gets processed. It's the clearest example in this course of an outside design philosophy becoming a regulation's actual text.

Retrofitting privacy into a system never built for it is expensive and incomplete. Building it in from day one is both cheaper and easier to trust. That closes out Chapter One. Next up: data classification concepts, where Chapter Two begins.
